rv.q: Its insistence on radical empathy shines bright.
Her play is a call to action that fizzes with rage and protest.
At the National, Martinez’s Jess, played with great warmth and wit by the author in Ian Rickson’s staging, has cerebral palsy (though Martinez prefers to describe herself as “wobbly”).
It’s exhilarating to see how much the National Theatre has invested in bringing so many disabled artists to the stage, at a time when their voices are so needed.
As a piece of drama it is worryingly weak: repetitive, simplistic and wildly overlong.
A play that sets out rightly to challenge the idea of normality, justly to take on government negligence, weakens its accomplishments by turning drama into dilemma.
This remains a compelling piece of work, in which a huge and theatrically under-represented sector of the British population – 14.6 million people according to Scope – takes centre stage.
Though the main characters are vividly drawn, they’re essentially dramatised case studies; the issue, or the cause, is always competing for attention with the people.
This drama may have aimed to cast light on the grim realities of life on the margins, but in the end it came dangerously close to a Twitter rant.
Well before the end, alas, the show goes down a partisan plughole, squandering political sympathy and losing its dramatic poise.
All of Us is a cry from the heart and a stimulating piece of theatre.
There can be few taboo subjects which induce the level of instantaneously awkward and uncomfortable human interactions than confronting unexpected physical disability.

Francesca Martinez’s latest play All of Us in the Dorfman is a ferocious statement about living with a disability and the deliberate erosion of independence that dehumanising government social care and economic policies have created.
But as the play divulges, it loses its emotional touch and begins to deteriorate into a soapbox for reactionary remarks.
The shows seems to come to a natural end at least twice before it finally finishes and at three hours long it could really do with a trim.
All of Us is written in a deeply committed and compassionate way, but although I agree with its political points, and am moved by some of its scenes, I also think that it’s not entirely problem-free.
It’s an ambitious, and slightly over-long, debut play from Martinez, which perhaps wisely doesn’t come up with a manifesto of its own to address the problems it raises.

cn.t: Martinez's passionate debut about disability and austerity divides critics: some praise its humor, anger, and vital subject matter, while others find it overlong, repetitive, and more polemic than drama at nearly three hours.
